section.title: Edom's Violence Against Jacob
section.sectionRationale: Here the oracle states the charge behind the sentence. On the day Jerusalem fell, Edom did not stand up for its brother Jacob; it stood aloof, then gloated, then joined the looting and even hunted down the fugitives. Six times the prophet hammers the phrase the day of their distress, exposing the treachery of a brother.
section.thesis: Edom's crime was the betrayal of a brother in his worst hour: standing by, cheering the ruin, seizing the plunder, and cutting off the escaping survivors, so its own shame and cutting off are just.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the summary charge of violence against brother Jacob, covered with shame; and the drumbeat of what Edom did on the day, aloof, gloating, looting, and blocking the fugitives.

units.label: The charge: violence against a brother
units.note: covered with shame, cut off forever

verses.text: Because of the {{chamas|violence}} against your {{ach|brother}} Jacob, you will be covered with shame and cut off forever.
On the {{yom|day}} you stood aloof while strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gate and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were just like one of them.
But you should not gloat in that day, your brother’s day of misfortune, nor rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their destruction, nor boast proudly in the day of their distress.
You should not enter the gate of My people in the day of their disaster, nor gloat over their affliction in the day of their disaster, nor loot their wealth in the day of their disaster.
Nor should you stand at the crossroads to cut off their fugitives, nor deliver up their survivors in the day of their distress.

chamas.gloss: Violence, wrong, cruel injustice. It is the same word that filled the earth before the flood, Genesis 6:11, and describes bloodshed and oppression against the helpless. Edom's chamas against its brother is the specific crime for which judgment is announced.

ach.gloss: Brother. The word insists on the family bond between Edom and Israel, the sons of the twin brothers Esau and Jacob. To call the victim your brother Jacob turns Edom's crime from mere enmity into betrayal of kin, deepening its guilt.

yom.gloss: Day. Obadiah repeats this word like a hammer blow through verses 11 to 14, the day of misfortune, destruction, distress, and disaster. The relentless drumbeat fixes attention on that one terrible day when Jerusalem fell and Edom chose the wrong side, and it sets up the greater Day of the LORD in verse 15.

basic.context: This is the heart of the accusation. When Jerusalem was attacked and fell, Edom did not help its relatives; it stood back and watched, then celebrated, then joined in the looting, and even blocked the roads to catch those trying to escape. Because Edom did violence to its brother, God says it will be covered with shame and cut off.
basic.hermeneutics: The passage lists real actions Edom took on the day of Jerusalem's fall, most likely in 586 BC. The prophet repeats the day again and again to drive home the horror of kicking a brother when he is down. What is condemned here, gloating over another's ruin and profiting from it, is condemned for anyone.
basic.originalLanguages: The crime is chamas, violence, the same word for the cruelty that filled the earth before the flood. The victim is called your brother, ach, which turns enmity into betrayal of family. And the word day, yom, is repeated like a drumbeat, ten times in these verses, fixing the eye on that one terrible day.
basic.typology: Edom betraying its brother in his hour of need is a dark picture of the world's cruelty toward God's suffering people, and even a faint echo of a friend turned traitor, answered ultimately at the cross where Christ was handed over.
basic.christ: Christ is the true brother who, unlike Edom, does not stand aloof from His people in distress but enters into their suffering to rescue them. Where Edom handed over the survivors, Jesus lays down His life so that not one of His own is lost.
basic.god: We learn that God notices how we treat others in their worst moments, especially the vulnerable. He takes the side of the afflicted, calling Judah My people, and He holds the bystander who gloats as guilty as the invader.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 137 remembers Edom crying tear it down over Jerusalem. Ezekiel 35 and Amos 1 also indict Edom for its cruelty. Proverbs 24:17 warns against rejoicing when your enemy falls.
basic.oneStory: Edom's betrayal of its brother is the crime at the centre of Obadiah. It shows the world's hostility to God's people at its ugliest, and it sets up the reversal to come: the God who sees the wrong will repay it and deliver His own.

context.literary:
Verses 1 to 9 announced Edom's fall; verses 10 to 14 stop to say why. The shift is marked by the little word 'because' at the start of verse 10, and from there the oracle changes its grammar. The first half spoke of what God will do to Edom, in the future tense. This block speaks to Edom directly and looks backward, and it does so with a long run of negative clauses, verses 12 to 14, eight of them in the Hebrew, each beginning 'do not' or 'nor'. The effect is of a prosecutor walking a witness through the day hour by hour.

The passage has a clear shape. Verse 10 is the thesis, naming the crime and the sentence together. Verse 11 is the first scene, in the past tense, and it contains two acts: standing apart, and being 'like one of them'. Verses 12 to 14 then come in three triplets. The first, verse 12, concerns the eyes and the mouth, looking on with pleasure and boasting. The second, verse 13, concerns the feet and the hands, entering the gate and looting. The third, verse 14, concerns the roads, blocking the escape and handing over the survivors. Each step is a little worse than the last, moving from attitude to word to deed to betrayal.

The refrain of the 'day' binds the whole thing, and note how it is varied. It is 'the day', then 'your brother's day of misfortune', then 'the day of their destruction', 'the day of their distress', 'the day of their disaster' three times, and 'the day of their distress' again to close. The Hebrew vocabulary for calamity keeps changing while the word 'day' stays fixed, so the reader feels one terrible day seen from many angles. That same word is about to be turned around in verse 15, where 'the day of the LORD' arrives for Edom.
context.historical:
The background is a quarrel older than the nation. Esau and Jacob were twins whose rivalry began in the womb, Genesis 25:23, and Esau's murderous grudge over the blessing, Genesis 27:41, was healed, at least for a moment, in the embrace of Genesis 33:4. Esau's line settled in Seir, the rugged country south and east of the Dead Sea, and 'Esau, that is, Edom' became a nation, Genesis 36:1. Israel was told to treat these people as kin: 'You will pass through the territory of your brothers, the descendants of Esau,' Deuteronomy 2:4, and 'Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother,' Deuteronomy 23:7. Yet Edom had refused Israel passage in the wilderness even when Moses addressed the Edomite king as 'your brother Israel,' Numbers 20:14-21.

The centuries after were marked by war. David subdued Edom, 1 Chronicles 18:12-13, and in the days of Jehoram Edom 'rebelled against the hand of Judah and appointed their own king,' 2 Kings 8:20-22. Under Ahaz the Edomites again 'attacked Judah and carried away captives,' 2 Chronicles 28:17.

The event Obadiah has in view is usually taken to be the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 586 BC. The other prophets and the Psalms line up behind that date. The singer of Psalm 137:7 asks the LORD to remember what the sons of Edom said that day, 'Destroy it, tear it down to its foundations!' Lamentations 4:21-22 tells Edom to 'rejoice and be glad' while warning that the cup will pass to her. Ezekiel 35:5 says Edom 'delivered the Israelites over to the sword in the time of their disaster.' Some scholars place Obadiah earlier, at a raid on Jerusalem in the reign of Jehoram, and the debate below weighs both. What neither view disputes is the outline of the sin: a kinsman who should have been a protector became a scavenger.
context.canonical:
Obadiah's charge is not a lone voice. It is part of a sustained biblical case against Edom, and reading the chorus together shows how heavily the memory of this day weighed on Israel. Amos 1:11 had earlier said Edom 'pursued his brother with the sword and stifled all compassion.' Joel 3:19 gives the same sin the same name, 'the violence done to the people of Judah, in whose land they shed innocent blood.' Ezekiel 25:12 says Edom 'acted vengefully against the house of Judah,' and the whole of Ezekiel 35 is given to Mount Seir. Malachi 1:2-4, a century or more after the fall, shows that the shadow lingered: 'Was not Esau Jacob's brother?' the LORD asks, and the brotherhood is again the sharpest edge of the question.

Isaiah gives Edom a larger role. In Isaiah 34:5-6 the LORD's sword comes down on Edom and the slaughter at Bozrah is a sacrifice; in Isaiah 63:1-3 a figure comes 'from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments' treading the winepress alone. In both, Edom stands for the nations that oppose God's people, which is why Obadiah can move from Edom to 'all the nations' in verse 15.

The positive side of the canon matters as much. Amos 9:12 promises that Israel will 'possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name,' and James quotes the Greek form of that promise at the Jerusalem council, Acts 15:16-17, to explain why Gentiles are welcomed without circumcision. The enemy named in Obadiah becomes a picture of the outsiders God brings in. The New Testament also turns the sin of Obadiah 11 into an ethic: the priest and Levite who 'passed by on the other side,' Luke 10:31-32, repeat in small the stance of standing apart, and Paul's 'Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep,' Romans 12:15, is the inverse of the gloating of verse 12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Obadiah wrote to people who had lost everything and were tempted to believe that nobody had noticed. The exiles and the survivors in Judah had watched a relative loot their ruins. The prophet's first purpose is to tell them that the whole day was seen and recorded, down to the detail of who stood at the crossroads. Notice how much he says by sheer specificity: he does not content himself with 'Edom was cruel'. He names the standing aside, the smirk, the boast, the walk through the gate, the hand on the goods, the ambush at the pass. A wronged people needs to hear the wrong named exactly, and a catalogue like this is a form of comfort.

His second purpose is to teach what kinship owes. By hammering the word 'brother' and the name 'Jacob', he says that closeness raises the bar. A stranger who plunders is a thief; a brother who watches, gloats and profits is a traitor. The standing in the family is the very thing that makes the sin heavy.

His third purpose is to make Judah ready for the verses that follow. The same people who suffered are being asked to trust that the LORD's sentence on Edom is fair and measured, that the shame and the cutting off of verse 10 answer exactly the shaming and the cutting off of verses 11 to 14. They are meant to hold their anger in God's hands and wait.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a historic wrong and the sentence on it. It does not give Judah permission to take vengeance, and it does not give later readers a warrant to treat any modern nation as Edom. The 'you should not' clauses are addressed to Edom, and they expose what a brother ought to have done by showing what Edom did.

What carries forward is the moral weight underneath. Scripture elsewhere states the same standard as direct instruction: 'Do not gloat when your enemy falls,' Proverbs 24:17, and 'Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep,' Romans 12:15. Obadiah adds two sharper lessons. First, standing aloof is not neutral when you are able to help and bound by kinship, a point Jesus makes in the story of the priest and the Levite, Luke 10:31-32. Second, profiting from another's collapse is a sin of its own, even when you did not cause the collapse. For the church the application starts close to home: how do we treat fellow believers in their hour of failure, and the people we have most reason to resent?

debates.question: Are the 'you should not' clauses commands, warnings, or an indictment of past acts?

views.label: A retrospective indictment
views.case: Read against the fall already described, the clauses catalogue what Edom actually did, gloating, looting, blocking escape. Verse 11 is plainly in the past, 'you stood aloof', and the negative form vividly relives the crime rather than forbidding a future one.

views.label: Prohibitions Edom violated
views.case: The Hebrew form is the ordinary way to say 'do not', so some read the clauses as the standing obligations of a brother that Edom trampled, its guilt lying in doing the very things it should never have done.

views.label: A prophetic warning that sees the day in advance
views.case: A smaller group takes the oracle as spoken before the event, so the clauses are real warnings and the past tense of verse 11 is a prophetic perfect. This fits an early date but strains the plain sense of verse 11.

debates.bearing: Either of the first two readings lands in the same place: Edom is guilty of these very acts, and the passage teaches both what a brother owes in the day of distress and what God will judge when it is withheld.

debates.question: Which disaster of Jerusalem does Obadiah describe?

views.label: The Babylonian conquest of 586 BC
views.case: Psalm 137:7, Lamentations 4:21-22 and Ezekiel 35:5 attribute Edom's glee and betrayal to that day. Obadiah's phrases about lots cast for Jerusalem and foreigners at the gate match a captured and plundered city, and the shared language with Jeremiah 49 suggests a prophet of the same period.

views.label: An earlier raid, in the reign of Jehoram
views.case: 2 Kings 8:20-22 and 2 Chronicles 21:16-17 record Edom's revolt and an invasion that plundered the king's household in the ninth century. Those who take this view point out that Obadiah never mentions the temple's burning or the exile of the king, as one might expect if Babylon were in view.

debates.bearing: The date changes the historical backdrop but not the message. Whichever disaster is meant, the offence is the same, and the later prophets confirm that Edom's hostility was a repeated pattern that came to a head in 586.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the word that frames the whole block, the 'because' at the head of verse 10, which says in one syllable that what follows is a reason and not a new subject. The sentence it opens has two verbs of sentence that deliberately mirror the crime. Edom will be 'covered', as it covered nothing for Judah, with shame, and 'cut off', the same verb of cutting that verse 14 uses of Edom cutting off the fugitives. The punishment is shaped like the offence.

The phrase 'were just like one of them' in verse 11 is the pivot of the whole passage. Two different words for outsiders have just been used, 'strangers' who carry off the wealth and 'foreigners' who enter the gate. Edom, who is neither, is declared to be one of them. A relative who stands aloof has chosen his side; the kin line has been erased by his own conduct, and the verse says so with the barest little word of comparison, 'like'.

Verse 12 is easy to read past. The BSB says 'you should not gloat', and the footnote on the last clause adds that the Hebrew says 'nor enlarge your mouth'. That is a vivid idiom for boasting, and it matches Ezekiel 35:13, where Edom 'boasted against Me with your mouth and multiplied your words against Me'. The gloating itself is rendered from a verb of looking, to look on with satisfaction. The sin starts in the eye and ends in the mouth, and the grammar keeps the two linked.

Then comes the run of negatives. They are built from the Hebrew word for 'not' that is used for prohibition rather than simple denial, and this is why English versions render them 'you should not' or 'do not'. Prohibitions in this form are the stuff of law and wisdom, which gives the section a weight of standard: Edom is being measured against something it should have known. In verse 13 'the gate of My people' stands out, because the possessive is God's own: Judah is His people, and the gate Edom walked through was His. To loot the gate is to trespass on something that belongs to God.

Finally, the 'cut off' of verse 14 describes Edom hunting 'fugitives' and 'survivors', two words for those who have slipped through the net. The first word is the ordinary one for the escaped; the second is the one the prophets love for the remnant that God keeps. Edom is therefore trying to destroy exactly the people through whom God means to preserve a future.

typology.type: The brother who turns on his brother
typology.fulfillment: Esau and Edom are one line of a pattern that begins with Cain, 'Am I my brother's keeper?', Genesis 4:9, and runs through Joseph's brothers. The pattern finds its sharpest form when Jesus, in Gethsemane, is betrayed by one of His own and then deserted by the rest, 'everyone deserted Him and fled,' Mark 14:50. The type falls short in that Edom's treachery is mere malice, while Jesus's betrayal is taken up into the plan of redemption, Acts 2:23.

Edom's allies 'cast lots for Jerusalem' in verse 11, and Joel 3:3 uses the same picture of lots cast for God's people. The scene returns at the cross, where soldiers divide Christ's garments by lot, John 19:23-24, fulfilling Psalm 22:18. The suffering city and the suffering Messiah share one fate. The type falls short because the lots at the cross do not finish God's people; they fulfil a promise that leads to their salvation.

typology.type: The one who passes by on the other side
typology.fulfillment: Edom's standing aloof is the Old Testament form of the priest and Levite who 'passed by on the other side,' Luke 10:31-32. Jesus gives the answer in the Samaritan, the outsider who becomes the neighbour. The correspondence is of stance rather than of event, so it is a moral echo more than a strict type, but it shows how the gospel remakes the neighbour, who is no longer defined by blood but by mercy, Luke 10:36-37.

typology.type: The kinsman who owes help in the day of distress
typology.fulfillment: Israel's law knew the kinsman redeemer, who steps in to buy back a relative in trouble, Leviticus 25:25. Edom is the anti-redeemer. The role is fulfilled in Christ, who became one with us in flesh and blood, 'so that in every respect He had to be made like His brothers,' Hebrews 2:17, in order to rescue the family from its enemy. The limit of the pattern is that no human kinsman could pay the price that He pays.

study.christ:
Obadiah 11 to 14 shows exactly what a brother is not, and the New Testament shows exactly what Jesus is. The easiest way into the passage is to place the two lists beside each other.

Edom stood aloof. Christ drew near. 'Since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity,' says Hebrews 2:14, and the same chapter says that He is 'not ashamed to call them brothers,' Hebrews 2:11. Edom, who was entitled to the name, was ashamed in the worst sense of treating the family as outsiders; Jesus, who owed us nothing, took the name.

Edom gloated at his brother's day of misfortune. Christ wept over a city that was about to fall to Rome, Luke 19:41-44, and sympathised with our weaknesses, Hebrews 4:15. Edom looted the gate of God's people; Christ opened it, 'I am the gate,' John 10:9. Edom stood at the crossroads to cut off the fugitives; Christ stands as the way and says, 'whoever comes to Me I will never cast out,' John 6:37. Edom handed the survivors over; Christ keeps them, 'I have not lost one of those You gave Me,' John 18:9.

The passage also looks toward the cross in a subtler way. The cross was the day of Jesus's own distress. People stood looking on, the soldiers cast lots for His clothes, John 19:23-24, the crowds mocked, Psalm 22:7-8 and Mark 15:29-32, and His friends fled. Verses 11 and 12 describe what it feels like to be gazed at in disaster by those who ought to help, and Isaiah 53:3 says of Him that men 'hide their faces' from Him. He took the place of the brother who is abandoned, and by doing so He made peace even with the Edoms of the world. Paul can write that He 'has destroyed the barrier, the dividing wall of hostility,' Ephesians 2:14, and Amos 9:12, quoted in Acts 15:16-17, shows that this includes a share of Edom itself.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Edom is not a cipher for Satan or for Judas, and the passage should not be forced into a code. The link is a consistent moral contrast, drawn from the way the New Testament itself describes Jesus as the elder brother who acts as the kin of those in need.
study.god:
The passage says several things about God that are easy to miss because the verbs are all about Edom.

First, God keeps a record. The prosecution in verses 11 to 14 depends on exact knowledge of what Edom did, from the standing aloof to the lookout at the pass. Nothing was hidden because the nations looked away. The same God who 'heard' Edom's boasting in Ezekiel 35:13 sees every crossroad. This is deeply consoling to a suffering people and deeply sobering to anyone who thinks distance gives cover.

Second, God's justice is proportionate. The sentence in verse 10 is not generic anger; it mirrors the sin. Edom shamed a brother and will be covered with shame; Edom cut off fugitives and will be cut off. This is the lex talionis at the level of nations, the same measure Scripture elsewhere applies to Babylon, Revelation 18:6. God is not capricious or excessive; He gives exactly what the crime deserves, and He gives it openly, with reasons.

Third, God takes sides without being partisan. He speaks of Judah as 'My people', and that possessive is why Edom's crime is also a crime against Him. Yet the book is not simply ethnic favouritism. Edom was told to treat Israel as kin, Deuteronomy 23:7, and was condemned for failing to. The God who gave Esau his mountain, Deuteronomy 2:5, holds Esau answerable for how he used it. His covenant love for Israel does not cancel His moral claim on everyone else.

Fourth, God's wrath is slow in coming and sure in arriving. The Edom story reaches back to Genesis and forward to Malachi. He did not strike at the first betrayal. He waited, sent warning through Amos, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and acted in His time.

For worship, the passage leads us to a God who cannot be bribed by distance or kinship, and it frees us from taking vengeance. Because He sees the day, we can leave the day with Him. Romans 12:19 says as much, and the Psalms that ask 'Remember, O LORD' do so because the matter is in His hands. The tension left open is how this sits with His patience and His mercy to the nations, a tension the later verses of Obadiah, and the book of Jonah, begin to answer.

crossReferences.note: Centuries earlier Moses addressed the king of Edom as 'your brother Israel' and begged only for passage along the King's Highway. Edom refused with an army. Obadiah's charge has a long root: the kinsman who would not help in the wilderness would not help in the siege.

'Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother.' Israel was commanded to honour the kinship, which makes the verdict on Edom more pointed: God asked of Israel the very fraternal loyalty that Edom withheld, and He recorded the failure.

The exiles by Babylon's rivers remember what the sons of Edom said on the day Jerusalem fell, 'tear it down to its foundations'. Obadiah and the psalmist describe one event from two sides: the prophet gives the verdict, the singer gives the grief.

Edom is told to rejoice for now, because the cup will pass to her as well. It sets the gloating of Obadiah 12 inside a larger judgment on Judah's own sin, and warns that mocking someone else's ruin does not exempt a person from the same cup.

Edom 'harbored an ancient hatred' and delivered the Israelites to the sword in the time of their disaster. Ezekiel names the long-standing root of Edom's hostility, tracing the day of Obadiah 11 back to a grudge that went all the way to Esau.

Edom 'pursued his brother with the sword and stifled all compassion'. The prophet who preceded Obadiah by generations already framed the sin as a loss of the pity that kinship demands, which the crossroads of Obadiah 14 shows in action.

The wisdom tradition states the rule Edom broke. Do not gloat when your enemy falls, because the LORD sees and may turn His wrath away from him. It adds a danger Obadiah only implies: the one who rejoices at another's fall draws God's attention to himself.

The priest and the Levite saw the wounded man and passed by on the other side. It is Obadiah 11 in a parable: standing aloof while a brother is in trouble. Jesus's answer, the Samaritan who stops, shows what Edom should have been.

The One who sanctifies and those He sanctifies are of one family, so Jesus is not ashamed to call them brothers. This is the New Testament's counter to Edom: a brother who, unlike Esau's line, does not abandon his family in their day.

Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Paul's one-line rule is the positive form of the whole of Obadiah 12 to 14, and it shows how the principle passed from the prophets into the church's everyday ethic.

study.oneStory:
Obadiah 10 to 14 belongs to a story that begins long before Edom was a nation. Brother against brother is the shape of the first human sin outside Eden: Cain rose against Abel, Genesis 4:8, and God asked, 'Where is your brother?' The question haunts the Bible. Jacob and Esau carry the same feud into the patriarchs, Joseph's brothers sell him, and now Edom turns on Judah. Each time God's answer is that He is the keeper of the wronged.

That is why the passage matters for creation and fall. Genesis 6:11 says the earth was 'full of violence', the same Hebrew word as the crime in Obadiah 10. Violence against kin is what the fall looks like when it has grown up, and the flood-world is the first place the word appears. So Obadiah's catalogue is a small portrait of how sin works in human families, nations and neighbours: it begins with looking away, grows into smiling at the loss, and ends in taking the spoil.

The same passage looks forward. It sets up the verses of Obadiah 15 to 21, where the Day of the LORD turns on Edom and the nations and Zion is restored. It also looks to the New Testament, where a better Brother has entered the family's worst day. The cross is the place where the old pattern is broken. Christ takes the humiliation of the betrayed, and by His resurrection He makes a new family in which Jew and Gentile, even Edomite and Judahite, are one body, Ephesians 2:14-16. The Edom that once barred the road to Israel becomes part of the 'remnant of Edom' that Amos 9:12 says will be possessed, and Acts 15 reads as a gathering in.

In the new creation there is no more standing aloof. Revelation 21:4 promises that 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain', and the nations walk by the light of the city, Revelation 21:24. The day of distress in verses 11 to 14 is the opposite of that city. It is the world as it is under the fall, where no brother can be trusted. The final world is one where every brother can.

sermon.why: No sermon on Obadiah 1:10-14 from a trusted expositor could be confirmed by web search in this session, so none is listed.

quiz.q: What is the specific crime for which Edom is condemned in this passage?

options.text: Violence against its brother Jacob on the day of Jerusalem's ruin.
options.note: Verse 10 names the violence against your brother Jacob as the ground of judgment.

options.text: Worshipping idols instead of the LORD.
options.note: Idolatry is condemned elsewhere, but here the charge is violence against a brother.

options.text: Failing to pay tribute to Judah.
options.note: No tribute is in view; the crime is betrayal of a brother in distress.

options.text: Refusing to trade with Jerusalem.
options.note: The charge is violence and treachery, not a trade dispute.

quiz.q: How did Edom act on the day Jerusalem fell?

options.text: It stood aloof, gloated, joined the looting, and cut off those trying to escape.
options.note: Verses 11 to 14 trace this escalation from bystander to active betrayer.

options.text: It sent soldiers to defend Jerusalem's gates.
options.note: The opposite: Edom entered the gate to loot, not to defend.

options.text: It quietly mourned but did nothing.
options.note: It did far worse than passive mourning; it gloated and plundered.

options.text: It sheltered the refugees who escaped the city.
options.note: It blocked and handed over the fugitives rather than sheltering them.

quiz.q: Why does the prophet keep repeating the phrase ‘the day of their distress’?

options.text: To fix attention on that one terrible day and the horror of betraying a brother in it.
options.note: The drumbeat of day, yom, drives home the weight of Edom's treachery.

options.text: To mark the many different days over many years.
options.note: It centres on one climactic day, not a spread of separate days.

options.text: Simply as a poetic filler with no real force.
options.note: The repetition is deliberate and heavy with meaning, not filler.

options.text: To predict the exact date of Edom's own fall.
options.note: It recalls Judah's day of ruin; it does not date Edom's fall.

quiz.q: What does calling the victim ‘your brother Jacob’ add to the charge?

options.text: It turns the crime from enmity into betrayal of kin, deepening Edom's guilt.
options.note: Edom and Israel descend from the twins Esau and Jacob, so this is treachery against family.

options.text: It simply gives a geographical location.
options.note: Jacob names the kindred people, not a place.

options.text: It shows the two nations had no relationship at all.
options.note: The point is the opposite: they are brothers, which makes it worse.

options.text: It softens the charge by appealing to family loyalty.
options.note: It does not soften the charge; the broken family bond makes it graver.

quiz.q: How does Christ stand in contrast to Edom in this passage?

options.text: He is the true brother who enters His people's distress to save them rather than standing aloof.
options.note: Hebrews 2 shows Christ unashamed to call us brothers, sharing our suffering to help us.

options.text: He, like Edom, keeps His distance until the danger passes.
options.note: The opposite is true: Christ draws near in suffering, unlike Edom.

options.text: He simply repeats Edom's judgment on all nations.
options.note: Christ does bring judgment, but the contrast here is His brotherly rescue.

options.text: He has no relationship to this passage at all.
options.note: Christ is the faithful brother the passage's failure points toward.

questions: Edom stood aloof while its brother suffered. Where might God be calling you to step in for someone in distress instead of watching from a safe distance?
The passage condemns gloating over another's downfall. Is there anyone whose troubles you have secretly enjoyed, and what would repentance look like there?
Edom profited from a brother's ruin. Are there ways you are tempted to gain from others' losses, and how does the gospel reshape that?
God called the sufferers My people and took their pain personally. How does it comfort you to know that God notices exactly how you are treated in your worst moments?
Christ is the brother who draws near in our distress rather than standing aloof. How can His nearness change the way you draw near to others who are hurting?

translationNotes.note: Cut off forever renders a phrase of decisive, lasting judgment; historically Edom did cease to exist as a distinct nation, its people displaced and absorbed by later centuries.
Cast lots for Jerusalem pictures the victors dividing the spoil and captives by lot; you were just like one of them equates the gloating bystander with the plundering foreigner.
Nor boast proudly renders a phrase the BSB footnote gives literally as nor enlarge your mouth, that is, do not speak arrogantly or gloat with open mouth over another's ruin.
The repeated you should not clauses, read against the fall already described, function as a vivid indictment of what Edom actually did, not merely as warnings for the future.
